newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish food sector hails export incentive decree.
newsitem.headline: Turkish food sector hails export incentive decree.

text.p: Turkish processed food producers welcomed a government decree which gives incentives to the export of several agricultural products in a bid to use up excess output and boost overall exports to close gaping trade deficits.

"We have been waiting for this decree for one-and-a-half years. It may cause jumps, maybe 100 percent, in Turkey's process foods exports," said Hakan Severge, general manager of Merko Gida which produces frozen and canned food.
"I think it is a big boost for the food sector," Severge told Reuters.

The export incentives, published in the Official Gazette and effective retroactively for the whole of 1997, will include olive oil, frozen fruits and vegetables, dry vegetables, preserves, fruit juices and flowers.
"The decision aims at facilitating compliance with the Common Agricultural Policy of the European Union (EU)," the Official Gazette said.
Turkey entered into a customs union with the EU from January 1996 and pledged to adapt its agriculture to the Common Agricultural Policy of the EU in five years to the year 2000.
Food industry analysts say Turkey's total food exports including processed and fresh were estimated at $1.5 billion in 1996, up from $1.35 billion a year ago.
Turkey's total foreign trade deficit is expected to show a surge to $20 billion in 1996, up sharply from $14.1 billion in 1995.

Severge said the pace of rises in total food exports had slowed in 1996 after the government stopped all export incentives on processed food items at the end of 1995 ahead of the planned customs deal.
"The producers then began working almost at half capacity. But any rise in production due to these incentives can easily be met by the existing idle capacities," he said.

Olive producers said the decree would help use up the record oilve oil production of 223,500 tonnes in 1996/97 in Turkey, against an output of 50,000 tonnes a year ago and consumption of only about 45,000 tonnes expected this year.
"We all are happy about the decree," said Cahit Cetin, head of olives and olive oil department at Turkey's biggest farmer cooperative, Taris.
"Olive oil producers have a capacity to export some 100,000 tonnes this year in view of the record production and the latest incentive package," he told Reuters.
He said Canada, Italy, Spain, the United States were among the probable customers of the Turkish olive oil, produced mainly in the Aegean regions.
He said Turkey's olive oil production would continue to rise next year, but did not give any estimates.

The exporters will benefit from the incentive scheme through deductions to be made by the central bank from their input spendings such as energy, corporate tax and workers' insurance premiums, not through direct cash refunds.
Severge said the decree would also help reduce tax evasion in the agricultural sector, which analysts say has the greatest share in Turkey's unregistered black economy.
"Those who want to benefit from the incentives will have to get their deals registered for the central bank's processing," he said.

The decree brings incentives ranging from $54 per tonne (for preserves) to $375 (for dry vegetables). It will not apply to any re-exports or exports carried out through border or coastal trade and free trade zones, according to the Official Gazette.
